activities.anchor: People spend roughly ninety per cent of their lives indoors
activities.caption: call the share — life lived inside
activities.name: idIndoorsEstimate

config.prompt: Roughly what share of our lives do we spend indoors?
config.why: About ninety per cent — which means interiors quietly set the terms of daily life: whether a kitchen is a pleasure or a bruising negotiation, whether a clinic calms or alarms, whether an office supports focus or fragments it.
config.context: Decoration chooses cushions; interior design decides where the door swings and how wide the path past the table runs.

activities.anchor: are the raw materials of any interior
activities.caption: file each effect under its element
activities.name: idElementBuckets

config.prompt: The elements at work — file each effect under the element that causes it:

items.label: horizontal lines read as calm and breadth
blues and greens calm and signal freshness
a rough limewash wall and a lacquered panel can share a colour and feel like different planets
carpet hushed and intimate; hard tile lively and echoing

config.why: Colour is the element with the strongest documented effect on perceived temperature and mood; light reveals all the others, and pattern adds rhythm at close range — rationed like strong spice.

activities.caption: pair each principle with its move
activities.name: idPrincipleMatch

config.prompt: The principles at work — pair each with its signature move:

pairs.right: two matching armchairs flanking a hearth — formal and stable
one large sofa offset by a cluster of smaller objects — modern and alive, harder to pull off
repetition with variation — a run of identical pendants, a floorboard stripe carrying the eye
one place to look first, usually by contrast of colour, scale or light
the test at the end: when all agree on a single idea, the room reads as designed rather than accumulated

config.why: Scale and proportion govern relationships: a ceiling feels high relative to the room's width, a chair feels right relative to the human body — and the rule of thirds is the traditional starting point for hanging art.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the rules and the rule-breakers
activities.name: idGrammarPredict

config.q: Celebrated designers visibly ignore the conventions. So what are the elements and principles, really?
choices: Grammar — the great iconoclasts break them knowingly and locally; beginners break them accidentally and everywhere
config.why: You can absolutely write in fragments — Eileen Gray, Carlo Scarpa, Kelly Wearstler break the conventions deliberately. Learn the rule, then choose.

activities.anchor: The test: if you cannot trace a design decision
activities.caption: drag the divider — styling, then design
activities.name: idConceptCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to produce a room — drag the divider:

before.label: Styling
before.text: Designed without a programme — attractive, occasionally lucky, and unaccountable when it fails.

after.label: Design
after.text: A concept — one controlling idea, such as 'the kitchen is the family's crossroads' — made hundreds of downstream decisions consistent: a generous island, durable materials, layered task light.

config.why: Trace every decision back to a programme line — otherwise you have made a decoration, not a decision.

activities.anchor: a work triangle (in kitchens, the stove–sink–fridge loop)
activities.caption: place the triangle total
activities.name: idTrianglePlace

config.prompt: A kitchen work triangle should total roughly how many metres?
config.why: Roughly 4 to 8 metres so steps are not wasted — and a path must never cut through a conversation area.

activities.anchor: Clearances are the quiet proof of a space plan
activities.caption: true or false — the clearance numbers
activities.name: idClearanceJudge

statements.s: A dining table needs roughly 90 cm of clear passage on each working side
statements.why: 60 cm will squeeze a body past a seated diner — 90 cm is the working clearance.

statements.s: Each diner claims about 60 cm of table edge
statements.why: The 60-cm-per-diner rule — the same number that governs the squeeze past a chair.

statements.s: A wheelchair needs a turning space around 150 cm across
statements.why: Law-adjacent: accessibility codes set minimums no aesthetic may violate.

statements.s: A doorway needs only 60 cm of clear width to be accessible
statements.why: 90 cm-plus clear width — the same number as the working-side passage.

statements.s: The clearance numbers come from designers' taste
statements.why: They come from anthropometrics — measured dimensions of human bodies — compiled in references such as Panero and Zelnik's Human Dimension and Interior Space.

activities.anchor: A typical commercial project moves through five
activities.caption: line up the five phases, brief first
activities.name: idProcessOrder

config.prompt: The project's five phases — order them, first phase first:
items: Programming — the research and brief, delivered as a written programme document the client signs
Schematic design — bubble diagrams and parti sketches, testing adjacencies at room scale
Design development — plans drawn to scale, materials and lighting selected, budgets attached
Construction documentation — the drawing set and specifications contractors bid and build from
Construction administration — submittal reviews, site visits, the punch list
config.why: Decisions get cheaper to change the earlier they are made — the process front-loads the thinking.
